questions.problem: Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A$ that correspond to eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ respectively. What is the general solution of the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution of our matrix differential equation is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-6{x}_{1}(t)-3{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -6 & -3\end{aligned}].$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ -6 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -6 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -6\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -6\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the system of differential equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=4{x}_{1}(t)-{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=2{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

*Hint: The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$*
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- We are given that the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]$ and ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]$ be eigenvectors of a matrix $A.$ Find the decoupling matrix of the differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we construct the matrix $E$, whose columns are the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}:$

$$
E=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, the decoupling matrix can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}D & ={E}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3\cdot (-3)-2\cdot (-4)}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -4 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=3{x}_{1}(t)+2{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Since $A$ is upper-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, we have $E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $x(t)=Eu(t)$, or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)={u}_{1}(t)-{u}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)={u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=6{x}_{1}(t)+7{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)-4{x}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution to a Linear System of Differential Equations

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Decoupling Substitution of a Linear System of Differential Equations
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the substitution that will decouple the following system of differential equations: 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=-3{x}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's construct the matrix differential equation $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)$ for the given system:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/b121e46eacd73987eb2d088f4b3904d293e267dd3a005cced0bfd85f55c5b300.svg)

We need to find the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of the matrix $A.$

- Since $A$ is lower-triangular, the eigenvalues are 

$$
\lambda_1=-3
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\lambda_2=1.
$$

- Let's go through the process of finding the eigenvectors.

- For $\lambda_1 =-3,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/b97a40ce65d174e23907ba00478f49f633ce1b2bf9fcb5fa3fb7627ed1e27d11.svg)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/a27de99267f5b34b0202c43b984c199264fd2b4808add80c2856bed984ab14f0.svg)

- For $\lambda_2 =1,$ we get 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/61d0d2e59d71dfc71df3bb0604165a54d52fc483196bd452a03a02cb33d0d9e3.svg)
So, we get an eigenvector 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/1acdb041f910f83f6cd7d17194e8ce25bc7e82020b55559ff5889b71e052a4c0.svg)

Therefore, we have ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/b50817ce9b7984b26e5099dfab0a6205dec82ff90d7069a87901dc92098ec905.svg)

Finally, the change of variables that decouples the system is given by $\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t),$ or equivalently,

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t)=4{u}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)=3{u}_{1}(t)+{u}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining the Decoupling Substitution of a Linear System of Differential Equations

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/72a4d6a819a56d80818184e16205028a3a51eab2e97d1cdad72b8d495e5fd8d1.svg)

It turns out that if the matrix $A$ has two *distinct real eigenvalues* $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, then $A$ is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

If the eigenvectors corresponding to $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ are ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

This result is true for any $n \times n$ system with $n$ distinct eigenvalues. We'll prove this result for a $2\times 2$ system at the end of the lesson.

Now, let's see some concrete examples.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/72a4d6a819a56d80818184e16205028a3a51eab2e97d1cdad72b8d495e5fd8d1.svg)

It turns out that if the matrix $A$ has two *distinct real eigenvalues* $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, then $A$ is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

If the eigenvectors corresponding to $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ are ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

This result is true for any $n \times n$ system with $n$ distinct eigenvalues. We'll prove this result for a $2\times 2$ system at the end of the lesson.

Now, let's see some concrete examples.

tutorials.name: Decoupling a Linear System of Differential Equations
tutorials.problem:
We've seen how to solve a decoupled system of differential equations. Our goal now is to understand in more detail why this method works. 

Let's consider our general linear system of two differential equations once again:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/6529692bc6317e2c675e756533a733c0caf087f3ac0b64b9c3a407924014d94b.svg)

We will show that if the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, we can convert it into an equivalent decoupled system.

If $A$ is diagonalizable, it has $2$ linearly independent eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$ We use these to form the *change of variables matrix* $E,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/c11833cbccd43c172ab7699a9000df5e2cf4bfedb0720958f1d5a407e5aeb8f2.svg)

Because the columns are linearly independent, $E$ is invertible. Then, the substitution  

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t)
$$

will transform our original system of differential equations into a decoupled one, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(Eu(t)) & =A(Eu(t)) \\ E{u}^{′}(t) & =AEu(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={E}^{-1}AE\,u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/c9657a197b8232d883c6da546170754f2cc6916378d0c269755b3b5aae2173e0.svg)

is a diagonal matrix, and ${\color{red}\lambda_1},$ ${\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ are the eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$

Following these steps, we now have the *decoupled system*
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/557b8775c900635024b99ba9123d8023b2667db0459b1c8df53df886f4b156f8.svg)

Here, the matrix $D = E^{-1}$ is sometimes called the **decoupling matrix**.

Let's see a concrete example.

tutorials.title: Decoupling a Linear System of Differential Equations
tutorials.content:
We've seen how to solve a decoupled system of differential equations. Our goal now is to understand in more detail why this method works. 

Let's consider our general linear system of two differential equations once again:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/6529692bc6317e2c675e756533a733c0caf087f3ac0b64b9c3a407924014d94b.svg)

We will show that if the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, we can convert it into an equivalent decoupled system.

If $A$ is diagonalizable, it has $2$ linearly independent eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$ We use these to form the *change of variables matrix* $E,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/c11833cbccd43c172ab7699a9000df5e2cf4bfedb0720958f1d5a407e5aeb8f2.svg)

Because the columns are linearly independent, $E$ is invertible. Then, the substitution  

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t)
$$

will transform our original system of differential equations into a decoupled one, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(Eu(t)) & =A(Eu(t)) \\ E{u}^{′}(t) & =AEu(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={E}^{-1}AE\,u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/c9657a197b8232d883c6da546170754f2cc6916378d0c269755b3b5aae2173e0.svg)

is a diagonal matrix, and ${\color{red}\lambda_1},$ ${\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ are the eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$

Following these steps, we now have the *decoupled system*
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/557b8775c900635024b99ba9123d8023b2667db0459b1c8df53df886f4b156f8.svg)

Here, the matrix $D = E^{-1}$ is sometimes called the **decoupling matrix**.

Let's see a concrete example.

tutorials.name: The Proof of the Formula For a General System
tutorials.problem:
Consider the $2\times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).
$$

 

Assume that $A$ is diagonalizable and has eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}$ with corresponding eigenvalues ${\color{red}\lambda_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\lambda_2},$ respectively.

We've been using the general solution formula 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But where does this formula come from? First, remember that the substitution

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/7ece1267196b62dfffdf40b16af1b94e9169b6a798f7841f0fd361733042764f.svg)

transforms the matrix differential equation into the equivalent decoupled system

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/a61af1176fb00e767ce5a8fc0ce349b79742937909f70c01701db56b126b010e.svg)

We can solve this new decoupled system using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the substitution $\mathbf{x}(t)=E\mathbf{u}(t)$, we can transform the system back to the variable $\mathbf x(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =Eu(t) \\  & =E({c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}E[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}E[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our original system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

tutorials.title: The Proof of the Formula For a General System
tutorials.content:
Consider the $2\times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).
$$

 

Assume that $A$ is diagonalizable and has eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}$ with corresponding eigenvalues ${\color{red}\lambda_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\lambda_2},$ respectively.

We've been using the general solution formula 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But where does this formula come from? First, remember that the substitution

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/7ece1267196b62dfffdf40b16af1b94e9169b6a798f7841f0fd361733042764f.svg)

transforms the matrix differential equation into the equivalent decoupled system

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14118344/assets/a61af1176fb00e767ce5a8fc0ce349b79742937909f70c01701db56b126b010e.svg)

We can solve this new decoupled system using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the substitution $\mathbf{x}(t)=E\mathbf{u}(t)$, we can transform the system back to the variable $\mathbf x(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =Eu(t) \\  & =E({c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}E[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}E[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our original system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$
